edits.old: BRAF-wild-type, controlled liver-only disease with a cleared primary has the strongest treatment evidence. KRAS mutation alone was allowed in TransMet (17/47 assigned LT), so a blanket KRAS ban would exceed evidence; that does not prove every molecular subgroup derives equal benefit. Arm D is a warning against stacking expansions. PET/Oslo/CEA markers forecast prognosis in recipients but have not demonstrated that crossing a threshold changes the incremental benefit of LT over modern non-LT care.
edits.new: BRAF-wild-type, controlled liver-only disease with a cleared primary has the strongest treatment evidence. RAS-mutant disease (including KRAS) was allowed in TransMet (17/47 assigned LT), so a blanket RAS ban would exceed evidence; that does not prove every molecular subgroup derives equal benefit. Arm D is a warning against stacking expansions. PET/Oslo/CEA markers forecast prognosis in recipients but have not demonstrated that crossing a threshold changes the incremental benefit of LT over modern non-LT care.

edits.old: Primary time origin was randomization. Median follow-up 59.3 months. Five-year ITT OS was 56.6% versus 12.6% (HR 0.37, 95% CI 0.21–0.65); per-protocol OS 73.3% versus 9.3%. Of 47 assigned LT, 38 received LT and 36 were per-protocol; nine had progression-related exclusion/dropout. The control arm included seven subsequent resections and two LT crossovers. Safety population comprised 40 grafted patients. Among 36 per-protocol LT recipients, 26 recurred; 19/26 received chemotherapy and 12/26 local curative-intent treatment. Median per-protocol PFS was 17.4 versus 6.4 months, and secondary PFS after salvage was 35.4 months in the LT arm. Three of 36 per-protocol recipients required retransplantation (primary nonfunction, donor gallbladder cancer, caval obstruction/large-for-size); one postoperative death was reported. Serious adverse events occurred in 32/40 safety LT recipients. Median wait to LT was 50.5 days, which limits transfer to longer-wait systems.

edits.old: TransMet's nine progression dropouts and three retransplants show why post-LT survival alone is inadequate. The 2026 SECA-II ten-year OS was 51.5%, not its five-year 77.8%; four metastatic deaths occurred after five years. Arm D's 18-month median OS cautions against assuming every expanded candidate obtains sufficient benefit. Selected HAIP/conversion patients can have durable survival without a graft, but cross-study comparisons cannot calculate an individual's LT gain.
edits.new: TransMet's nine non-transplanted LT-arm patients (eight progression/extrahepatic disease and one prostate cancer) and three retransplants show why post-LT survival alone is inadequate. The 2026 SECA-II ten-year OS was 51.5%, not its five-year 77.8%; four metastatic deaths occurred after five years. Arm D's 18-month median OS cautions against assuming every expanded candidate obtains sufficient benefit. Selected HAIP/conversion patients can have durable survival without a graft, but cross-study comparisons cannot calculate an individual's LT gain.

edits.old: Six months: international expert-guidance default, not US policy or a proven biological cliff. Reliable pre-referral stability may contribute.
edits.new: Six months: proposed local default informed by German DGVS/DGAV S2k guidance, not US policy, the international EHE consensus, or a proven biological cliff. Reliable pre-referral stability may contribute.

old.design_population: Prospective phase II experience: 61 potentially eligible atezolizumab–bevacizumab-treated patients; 16 enrolled/listed/transplanted responders.
old.selection: The 45 not included comprised 25 treatment discontinuations (15 progression, four adverse events, six decompensation) and 20 failing downstaging criteria. Eight of 16 had portal thrombosis, grades not verified; 15 had prior locoregional treatment.
old.results: Median washout 57.5 days (IQR 29–87), median follow-up 16 months. Acute rejection 4/16 (25%); three irAEs. Ninety-day morbidity 62.5%, mortality 1/16. Explants: ten complete and six partial responses; one recurrence. Two-year recipient OS 94%, RFS 90%.
old.limits: These are selected-16 outcomes, not 61-patient ITT efficacy. Small, nonrandomized, short follow-up; a shorter median washout does not establish safety. Retransplantation count was not independently extractable from accessible primary text and is not asserted.
old.locator: Published abstract plus accessible publisher Results, PMID 41763363; full PDF needed for eligibility, flow and adverse-event denominators.

new.design_population: Prospective single-centre observational cohort: 61 potentially eligible patients treated with atezolizumab–bevacizumab; 16 selected responders were enrolled, listed and transplanted.
new.selection: Among 45 not included, 25 discontinued treatment (15 progression, four adverse events, six decompensation) and 20 failed downstaging criteria. Eight of 16 had baseline portal-vein tumor thrombosis (six Vp2, one Vp3, one Vp4); 15 had prior locoregional treatment. These were selected research recipients, not proof of standard eligibility after vascular invasion.
new.results: Median washout 57.5 days (IQR 29–87), median follow-up 16 months. Four biopsy-confirmed acute rejections (25%); three irAEs. Ninety-day morbidity 10/16 and mortality 1/16; two retransplants. Explants: ten complete and six partial responses; one recurrence. Reported two-year OS 94% (95% CI 67–100) and recurrence-free estimate 90% (62–98) in the 16 recipients; Methods start both clocks at listing and censor death for recurrence, so the latter is not conventional recurrence-or-death RFS.
new.limits: Selected-16 outcomes, not efficacy among all 61 treated patients. Small, observational cohort with short follow-up. A shorter median washout does not establish safety. The fatal course included graft dysfunction, rejection, sepsis and retransplantation; graft loss should not all be attributed to rejection. Supplement and mechanistic analyses were not fully reviewed.
new.locator: J Hepatol2026;85:117–129. PMID41763363. PDF pp3–5 selection, flow and endpoint definitions; Figures1–3; p8 safety; Table2. Targeted main clinical read; supplement not reviewed.

files.old:
html: () => `

Reference standard: HVPG 10 mmHg or more, in viral and alcohol-related cirrhosis. Varices, ascites or portosystemic collaterals are clinical signs of portal hypertension.

Noninvasive (compensated advanced chronic liver disease): liver stiffness by transient elastography of 15 kPa or less with platelets 150 ×10⁹/L or more rules CSPH out; 25 kPa or more rules it in for viral, alcohol-related and non-obese NASH disease. Between these, ANTICIPATE estimates at least 60% risk at 20–25 kPa with platelets under 150, or 15–20 kPa with platelets under 110.

CSPH, by HVPG or clinical signs, raises the risk of decompensation and death after resection for HCC.

These are Baveno VII (2022) statements. The HCC roadmap follows the 2026 BCLC update; a later Baveno edition was not verified here.

${src(pm('35120736', 'de Franchis 2022 · Baveno VII'))}`},
files.new:
html: () => `

Reference standard: HVPG ≥10 mmHg in viral and alcohol-related cirrhosis. CSPH raises decompensation risk after HCC resection.

Baveno VIII (2026), compensated advanced chronic liver disease: LSM ≤15 kPa plus platelets ≥150 ×10⁹/L rules out CSPH. Diagnostic criteria, with their individual limitations, are ANTICIPATE/ANTICIPATE-NASH or NICER probability ≥75%; LSM ≥25 kPa for viral/alcohol-related disease or non-obese (BMI <30) MASLD; or spleen stiffness >55 kPa measured at 100 Hz. LSM refers to vibration-controlled transient elastography. Use ANTICIPATE-NASH for MASLD with obesity.

For indeterminate results, reassessment at 12 months may be preferred (weak recommendation; low-level evidence). HCC limits: noninvasive tests may not apply with macrovascular invasion. The LSM/platelet rule-out applies in BCLC 0–C; ANTICIPATE probability ≥75% is highly suggestive in BCLC 0–A without a right-lobe nodule >5 cm. Apply the clinical and imaging context.

${src(pm('42624290', 'Baveno VIII 2026 · statements 1.14–1.17, 1.21–1.23'), pm('35120736', 'Baveno VII · HVPG and resection risk'))}`},
